record.paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
record.original_question: What is the high-temperature regime of manganites well above room temperature and above T*: does a separate temperature scale Tpol mark the onset of individual polarons after charge-ordered clusters disappear, and does the system eventually become metallic again at still higher temperature?

evidence.quote: The regime of temperatures well above room temperature must be carefully explored, even beyond T*. At T >T *, the CO clusters are no longer formed but a gas of polarons may still be present. Perhaps this leads to another temperature scale, denoted by Tpol in Fig.4, where individual polarons start forming? Is the system metallic upon further increasing the temperature?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a hole-doped colossal-magnetoresistance (CMR) manganite of the form $\mathrm{R}_{1-x}\mathrm{A}_x\mathrm{MnO}_3$ (with $\mathrm{R}$ a trivalent rare earth and $\mathrm{A}$ a divalent alkaline earth, in the doping range where ferromagnetic-metallic and charge-ordered phases compete). Below a characteristic temperature $T^{*}$ (well above the ferromagnetic Curie temperature $T_C$) the system is known to host short-range, dynamic charge-ordered (CO) clusters of correlated polarons coexisting with a polaronic background.

Address the following questions about the regime $T \gg T_C$, in particular $T > T^{*}$ (well above room temperature):

(a) Once $T$ exceeds $T^{*}$ and the short-range charge-ordered clusters have dissolved, does there exist a further distinct temperature scale $T_{\mathrm{pol}} > T^{*}$ marking the onset (upon cooling from very high $T$) of individual, well-defined small polarons out of an essentially uncorrelated electron-phonon fluid? Equivalently, is the polaron formation temperature $T_{\mathrm{pol}}$ strictly separated from the cluster formation temperature $T^{*}$, or do the two scales coincide?

(b) At still higher temperatures $T > T_{\mathrm{pol}}$, does the manganite recover a metallic (non-polaronic, weakly correlated) transport regime, characterized by $d\rho/dT > 0$ and the absence of activated polaronic conduction?

Provide a theoretical and/or experimental determination of whether $T_{\mathrm{pol}}$ exists as a separate crossover and whether a high-temperature metallic phase is restored.
artifact.status_search_result: Searches indicate that while a polaron-correlation temperature T* (≈300 K in bilayer manganites) is well documented, the existence of a separate higher polaron-onset scale T_pol and a recovery of metallic behavior at still higher temperatures has not been conclusively established. Experimental work continues to find polaronic signatures persisting up to and even within the metallic phase, and no consensus on a distinct T_pol or a high-temperature metallic regime has emerged. The question therefore appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Formation and temperature evolution of correlated polarons in colossal magnetoresistive manganites
status_evidence.snippet: Short-range polaron correlations are completely dynamic at high temperature, then freeze upon cooling to T* ≈ 310 K.
status_evidence.claim: Establishes T* as a polaron-correlation freezing scale but does not identify a separate higher T_pol or a high-T metallic phase.

status_evidence.title: Bilayer manganites reveal polarons in the midst of a metallic breakdown
status_evidence.snippet: Polarons identified in the metallic phase of manganites down to 6 K.
status_evidence.claim: Polaronic signatures persist into the metallic state, complicating any clean separation of T_pol from T* or a simple high-T metallic crossover.

status_evidence.title: Polaron melting and ordering as key mechanisms for colossal resistance effects in manganites
status_evidence.snippet: Polaron melting and ordering proposed as key mechanisms for CMR.
status_evidence.claim: Supports clustered/polaronic picture but does not resolve the existence of a separate T_pol scale above T*.
